R001.fact: For an at most countable indexed family of sets with nonnegative extended real costs, one can preserve every index once in an enumeration by natural numbers, padding unused positions by empty sets of cost zero. The union and total cost are unchanged. Conversely every sequence is a countable cover. This remains valid for an empty or finite family and for an infinite total cost.

grounds.reason: D002 uses countable covers with nonnegative costs and zero cost for empty members.
M001 uses sequences indexed by natural numbers, with the same zero cost for empty members.
S001 compares precisely these two cover presentations at a fixed finite positive scale.

R001.justification: Inject the countable index set into ℕ, place each original member at its assigned position, and put ∅ elsewhere. Union membership is unchanged. A sum of nonnegative terms is the supremum of its finite subsums, which are unchanged by this injection and zero padding. Thus the comparison preserves costs even when the sum is infinite; no enumeration of the covered set A is involved.

R001.fact: For a finite scale δ>0 and s>0 in Euclidean space, every set U with extended diameter at most δ has a finite diameter d∈[0,δ]. On nonempty U its extended nonnegative real power d^s is the image of the ordinary real power, including 0^s=0; empty members have zero cost by the stated conventions.

grounds.reason: The ambient space is Euclidean R^m for an arbitrary natural m.
The exponent s is a positive real.
D001 identifies finite extended Euclidean diameter with its ordinary nonnegative real value.
D002 restricts each cover member's diameter to the positive real scale δ and assigns zero empty-set cost.
M001 has the same diameter restriction and explicitly assigns empty-set cost zero.

R001.justification: A nonempty such U is bounded: fixing x∈U, every y∈U satisfies dist(x,y)≤diam(U)≤δ. Its distance supremum is therefore finite and agrees with D001's real diameter. On a positive finite d, both real-power conventions use exp(s log d), and at d=0 both give zero because s>0. Together with the separate empty-set rule, the two formulas have equal costs on every admissible member.

R002.fact: A compact subset K of Euclidean R^n is bounded and is contained in [-b,b]^n for some real b>0, also when n=0.

grounds.reason: H003 states that E is compact in the specified Euclidean space.
n is natural and E is a Euclidean subset.

R002.justification: The unit balls centered at points of K cover K, hence finitely many suffice by compactness. The triangle inequality bounds the norm of every covered point by 1 plus the maximum norm of the finitely many centers (including 0 in this maximum handles an empty family). Each absolute coordinate is at most the Euclidean norm, so increasing the finite bound to a positive b gives the coordinate box. In R^0 the coordinate conditions are vacuous.

R002.fact: For b>0, n>0 and 0<h<=1, the box [-b,b]^n has a finite cover by at most (2b+2)^n h^(-n) coordinate boxes, each of Euclidean diameter at most sqrt(n)h.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies the positive box bound.
S002 chooses b and imposes n>0 and 0<h<=1 before constructing the partition.

R002.justification: Put k=ceil(2b/h), a positive integer, and split each interval into k equal closed subintervals of length 2b/k<=h. There are k^n product boxes. The ceiling bound gives k<=2b/h+1<=(2b+1)/h<=(2b+2)/h. For two points in a box each coordinate difference has absolute value at most h, so their squared Euclidean distance is at most n h^2. Thus the asserted diameter bound holds. Calling these boxes cubes does not affect either estimate.

R002.fact: For fixed positive finite K and p, K h^p tends to zero as h tends to zero through positive values. For n>0 and a>n, the displayed cover costs C h^(-n)(sqrt(n)h)^a equal C n^(a/2)h^(a-n); the associated diameter bound sqrt(n)h also tends to zero.

grounds.reason: Here C=(2b+2)^n is positive finite, n>0, a>n, and h>0; hence p=a-n>0 and K=C n^(a/2)>0 are finite.

R002.justification: The positive-real power laws give the cost identity. For any epsilon>0, choosing 0<h<(epsilon/K)^(1/p) gives K h^p<epsilon, by monotonicity and inverse identities for positive powers. For any fixed delta>0, additionally choosing h<=delta/sqrt(n) ensures the diameter bound is at most delta. These choices can also satisfy h<=1. Thus for every fixed delta the nonnegative defining infimum is below every positive epsilon, so it is zero; taking the supremum of these zero contents gives H^a(E)=0. This justifies the limit passage already used in S002 without interchanging an infimum and supremum.

R002.fact: For an extended nonnegative number d and finite real t>=0, if d<=a for every finite real a>t, then d<=t and d is finite. In particular, if d<=s for every positive real s, then d=0.

grounds.reason: N001 has yielded D<=a for arbitrary a>n in the n>0 branch; n is finite and nonnegative.
N001 gives nonnegativity of dimension.

R002.justification: The test a=t+1 first excludes d=infinity. If the finite value d were greater than t, the real midpoint (t+d)/2 would contradict the assumed bound. For t=0 combine the resulting upper bound with nonnegativity. Thus no real identification of D is required before proving its finiteness.

R002.fact: If K is a compact Euclidean set and s,delta>0, the balls B(x,delta/2), x in K, admit a finite subcover whose members have diameter at most delta and finite total s-cost.

grounds.reason: H003 provides compactness of E.
S004 fixes arbitrary positive real s and delta and selects these balls.
D001 defines diameter as the supremum of distances.
D002 permits finite covers as countable covers and defines scale content as their cost infimum.

R002.justification: Each ball is open and contains its center because delta/2>0, so these balls cover K. Compactness supplies finitely many of them. For any two points in a selected ball the triangle inequality gives distance less than delta, so the supremum of distances is at most delta. Each diameter therefore has finite nonnegative s-power, and the finite sum is finite. If an infinite indexing is desired, append empty sets with zero cost. The scale-content infimum is at most this finite sum.

R003.fact: For a>1, N^(1-a) tends to 0 and 1/N tends to 0 as positive integers N tend to infinity. Consequently, for every delta>0 and eta>0 there is N with 1/N<=delta and N^(1-a)<eta. The intervals [k/N,(k+1)/N], 0<=k<N, cover [0,1] and each has diameter 1/N.

grounds.reason: The step fixes a>1 and ranges over positive integers N.
I is [0,1] with Euclidean distance.
The scale content is the infimum over countable covers with diameter at most delta.

R003.justification: Writing b=a-1>0, the standard real power function t^b is increasing and unbounded on positive t, so N^(-b) tends to zero; the Archimedean property selects N beyond both required thresholds. Consecutive endpoints establish the finite cover and the endpoint distance equals its diameter. Padding by empty sets makes it countable. Nonnegativity and arbitrarily small admissible costs give zero content for each delta, hence zero supremum over scales.

R003.fact: A nonempty subset B of R with finite diameter r is bounded and has real endpoints l=inf B and u=sup B with u-l=r. For h>0, B is contained in (l-h,u+h), whose Lebesgue length is r+2h. Thus the J_i in S002 exist and have length rho_i+epsilon*2^(-i-1) for nonempty V_i, and length zero for empty V_i.

grounds.reason: Each covering set has diameter rho_i<=delta<infinity, and epsilon>0.
J_i uses h=epsilon*2^(-i-2), positive for every natural i.
Diameter is the supremum of pairwise distances.
Lebesgue interval lengths have their usual values.

R003.justification: Choosing x in B gives |y-x|<=r for all y in B and thus boundedness. Completeness supplies l,u. Every pairwise distance is at most u-l; points arbitrarily close to both endpoints show the reverse diameter inequality by taking their errors to zero. The strict enlargement contains the endpoints and B. Subtracting its endpoints gives r+2h. No measurability of B is needed.

R003.fact: For a countable cover I subset union_i J_i by open intervals or empty sets, 1=lambda(I)<=sum_i lambda(J_i). For nonnegative sequences x_i,y_i, termwise inequalities pass to their extended sums and sum_i(x_i+y_i)=sum_i x_i+sum_i y_i. In particular sum_{i>=0}2^(-i-1)=1 and the constructed J_i imply 1<=sum_i rho_i+epsilon for every epsilon>0, hence sum_i rho_i>=1.

grounds.reason: J_i cover I, all J_i are open or empty, and their lengths have the displayed upper bound.
lambda is Lebesgue measure, and lambda([0,1])=1.
rho_i are nonnegative finite diameters.

R003.justification: Measure monotonicity and countable subadditivity yield the covering inequality. Subadditivity follows by disjointizing the measurable J_i and applying countable additivity; each disjoint piece has measure at most that of its original interval. Nonnegative sums are suprema of finite partial sums, which gives monotonicity and additivity. The geometric partial sums are 1-2^(-M), tending to 1. If T=sum rho_i is infinite the conclusion is immediate; if T<1, choosing epsilon=(1-T)/2 contradicts 1<=T+epsilon. This is exactly the epsilon removal in S002.

R003.fact: For delta>0 and 0<s<1, every r in [0,delta] satisfies r^s>=delta^(s-1)r, and delta^(s-1) tends to infinity as delta decreases to zero. Multiplication of a nonnegative extended sum by the positive finite number delta^(s-1) commutes with that sum. Therefore a common lower bound on all admissible cover costs bounds their infimum, and the resulting scale bounds make their supremum infinite.

grounds.reason: delta>0 and 0<=rho_i<=delta are available.
F002 gives sum rho_i>=1 under the cover assumption.
s is arbitrary with 0<s<1, and all covers are quantified before taking the scale supremum.
H_delta and H are respectively the cover infimum and positive-scale supremum.

R003.justification: For r>0, real power laws give r^s=r*r^(s-1), and the negative exponent makes r^(s-1)>=delta^(s-1); for r=0 both sides vanish because s>0. Extended-sum scaling follows from finite partial sums and their suprema, including infinity since the multiplier is strictly positive. Writing b=1-s>0 gives delta^(s-1)=1/delta^b, unbounded as delta tends to zero. Thus no exchange of limits or integrals is involved: every cover has the same lower bound, and these bounds exceed every finite number across positive scales.

R003.fact: For d in [0,infinity], if d<=a for every real a>1 and d>=s for every real 0<s<1, then d=1.

grounds.reason: Applying N001 after the zero-measure result gives the upper bounds for all a>1.
Applying N001 after the infinite-measure result gives the lower bounds for all 0<s<1.
Dimension is nonnegative.

R003.justification: The bound with a=2 makes d finite. If d>1, the midpoint (1+d)/2 violates the upper family; if d<1, the midpoint (d+1)/2 lies in (0,1) and violates the lower family. These order arguments justify the endpoint dimension conclusions without assuming continuity of dimension.

R004.fact: In the n=0 branch the coordinate map f:R→R^(0+1), f(t)=(x0,t), preserves distances, satisfies f(I)=F and preserves diameters of all covering sets. Thus countable covers transfer with the same positive-exponent costs and scales.

grounds.reason: Under n=0, E is the singleton R^0 and D=0.
The product distance reduces to |t-u| for the unique R^0 coordinate.
H^a(I)=0 for a>1.

R004.justification: For every t,u the displayed product distance equals |t-u|; taking suprema proves diameter preservation. Images commute with unions and remain countably indexed, so each admissible cover pushes to an admissible cover of F with identical cost. The formula defines the coordinate map on all R, including covering points outside I.

R004.fact: For a family of nonnegative extended-real costs with infimum zero, every eta>0 admits a member of cost <eta. A countable cover can be indexed by N, padding a finite cover by empty sets at zero cost.

grounds.reason: q>0, r>0 and H^q_r(E)=0 have been established; eta=epsilon/2>0.
The content is the infimum of costs of countable covers, with empty members costing zero.

R004.justification: The family is nonempty since the empty infimum is infinity. If no cost were below eta, eta would be a positive lower bound, contradicting infimum zero. Enumerating a countable family, or padding a finite one, gives the sequence used in F001 without changing coverage or cost.

R004.fact: A nonempty zero-diameter Euclidean set is a singleton. In R^n with n≥1, an open ball of radius b/2 for b>0 contains its center and has diameter b. For q>0 the declared beta_i is positive, beta_i≤r/2, and beta_i^q≤epsilon*2^(-i-3).

grounds.reason: The branch has n≥1 and q,r,epsilon>0.
beta_i is the minimum of r/2 and the positive q-th root of epsilon*2^(-i-3).

R004.justification: Distance zero forces any two points of a zero-diameter set to coincide. The triangle inequality gives ball diameter ≤b; points tending to opposite ends along any coordinate axis give distances tending to b, hence equality of the supremum. Positive real powers are increasing on nonnegative reals, and the positive q-th root has q-th power equal to its argument. These facts establish all replacement guards and costs.

R004.fact: For epsilon>0, sum_(i≥0) epsilon*2^(-i-3)=epsilon/4. Nonnegative countable sums are monotone under termwise domination and restriction of indices, and are additive for termwise sums and homogeneous for finite nonnegative scalars.

grounds.reason: The original q-cost is <epsilon/2.
Each singleton replacement adds a nonnegative cost at most epsilon*2^(-i-3); the other members are unchanged.

R004.justification: The finite geometric sum is (epsilon/4)(1-2^(-M-1)) for indices 0 through M, whose supremum is epsilon/4. Defining nonnegative series by suprema of finite partial sums proves monotonicity and scalar multiplication; additivity follows by taking common finite index supersets. Consequently the new total is at most the old total plus epsilon/4, hence strictly below epsilon.

R004.fact: For each i in countable K, finitely many intervals indexed by 1≤j≤N_i give a countable family of products. If diam(U_i)=r_i and each interval has length ≤r_i, each product has Euclidean diameter ≤sqrt(2)r_i. For r_i>0 and q>0, N_i≤2/r_i implies N_i(sqrt(2)r_i)^(q+1)≤2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)r_i^q, also after nonnegative summation.

grounds.reason: K⊆N, the U_i cover E, and 0<r_i≤r≤1 with finite sum of q-costs.
N_i=ceil(1/r_i) is positive and ≤2/r_i; its intervals cover I and have length ≤r_i.
F uses the Euclidean product distance.

R004.justification: The pairs (i,j) form a subset of N×N, so are countable. For points in a fixed product both coordinate distances are ≤r_i, and the product distance is therefore ≤sqrt(2)r_i. Monotonicity of positive real powers bounds each cost. The usual real-power laws for positive factors give the displayed termwise identity and inequality; taking suprema of finite subsums yields the series estimate. Product coverage follows by selecting an i covering x and then an interval covering t.

R004.fact: If a nonnegative extended real X satisfies X≤C*epsilon for every epsilon>0 with fixed 0<C<infinity, then X=0. If Y≤q+1 for every real q>D with finite D, then Y≤D+1; likewise Y≤a for all a>1 implies Y≤1.

grounds.reason: For fixed q and delta, F003 bounds the same content by C*epsilon with C=2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)>0 finite.
D is finite and nonnegative.
N001 yields dim_H(F)≤q+1 for arbitrary q>D.
In the zero-dimensional branch N001 yields dim_H(F)≤a for arbitrary a>1.

R004.justification: Taking epsilon=1 first excludes X=infinity. If X>0, epsilon=X/(2C) contradicts the bound. For the dimension bound, choosing q=D+1 first excludes Y=infinity. If finite Y>D+1, choose q=D+(Y-D-1)/2 to contradict Y≤q+1. The same midpoint argument gives the bound at 1 in the other branch. Supremum over zero contents is zero by the supplied definition, without any exchange of limits.

R005.fact: For the Euclidean product distance in D006, both coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz. Thus diam(A_i) and diam(B_i) are at most rho_i=diam(V_i). A nonempty B_i of finite diameter is bounded in R.

grounds.reason: The product distance is sqrt(||x-y||_2^2+|t-u|^2).
V is a delta-cover with finite positive delta, and A_i,B_i are its coordinate projections.
Diameter is the supremum of pairwise distances, with empty diameter zero.

R005.justification: Each coordinate distance is bounded by the product distance by nonnegativity of the other square. Lift any two projected points to V_i and take the supremum. If B_i is nonempty, fixing b in B_i gives |t-b|≤rho_i for every t in B_i, so it lies in the bounded interval [b-rho_i,b+rho_i].

R005.fact: A nonempty bounded B⊆R has finite a=inf B and b=sup B and diam(B)=b-a. For eta>0, J=(a-eta/2,b+eta/2) is open, contains B, and has Lebesgue length diam(B)+eta. Hence the J_i in S002 satisfy B_i⊆J_i and λ(J_i∩I)≤λ(J_i)≤rho_i+eta_i, also under the specified empty-set convention.

grounds.reason: Nonempty B_i are bounded and diam(B_i)≤rho_i.
eta_i is positive and J_i is defined by these endpoints or is empty.
λ is Lebesgue measure and intervals have their usual lengths.

R005.justification: Completeness of R supplies both extrema. All pairwise differences are at most b-a; points arbitrarily close to each extremum give the converse diameter bound, with the zero-width case immediate. The positive enlargement strictly contains both endpoints. Its interval length is b-a+eta, and measure monotonicity gives the intersection bound.

R005.fact: For fixed t∈I define W_i=A_i if t∈J_i and W_i=empty otherwise. These form a countable delta-cover of E, and sum_i diam(W_i)^s≤sum_i rho_i^s 1_(J_i)(t) for s>0. Consequently the defining infimum gives c≤sum_i f_i(t).

grounds.reason: V covers F and diam(A_i)≤rho_i≤delta.
B_i⊆J_i.
For x∈E and t∈I, (x,t)∈F.
H^s_delta is the infimum of these countable covering costs.

R005.justification: For each x∈E the cover supplies i with (x,t)∈V_i, which forces x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. On selected indices use monotonicity of u↦u^s on nonnegative reals; on other indices the empty-set cost is zero. Monotonicity of a nonnegative countable sum and the infimum lower-bound property prove the inequality. This makes the selection a sequence without requiring a reindexing.

R005.fact: For μ=λ|I, μ(R)=1. Each f_i=a_i 1_(J_i), a_i=rho_i^s finite and nonnegative, is Borel measurable and hence μ-almost-everywhere measurable, and ∫ f_i dμ=a_i λ(J_i∩I). If c≤g on I with c finite nonnegative and g nonnegative measurable, then c≤∫g dμ.

grounds.reason: I=[0,1] is Borel with Lebesgue length one.
λ and its restriction and nonnegative integral are specified.
Each J_i is open and measurable.
The f_i are nonnegative measurable and their sum dominates c on I.
c and each rho_i are finite nonnegative.

R005.justification: Restriction gives μ(A)=λ(A∩I) on Borel A and assigns zero measure to the complement of I. Indicators of measurable sets and their finite constant multiples are measurable; their simple-function integral is the coefficient times the measure. A nonnegative countable sum is measurable as the increasing supremum of its measurable partial sums. Integrating c 1_I≤g and using monotonicity and μ(I)=1 yields the lower bound.

R005.fact: For nonnegative sequences, countable sums preserve termwise inequalities and satisfy sum_i(u_i+v_i)=sum_i u_i+sum_i v_i, even when infinite. For the coefficients in S004, rho_i^s(rho_i+eta_i)=rho_i^(s+1)+eta_i rho_i^s and sum_i eta_i rho_i^s≤epsilon.

grounds.reason: rho_i is finite nonnegative.
s>0, epsilon>0 and eta_i=epsilon 2^(-i-1)/(1+rho_i^s).
Only nonnegative terms are summed.

R005.justification: A nonnegative series is the supremum of its finite initial sums, which proves monotonicity and additivity by passing from finite sums to their suprema. For positive rho_i the usual real-power addition law gives rho_i^s rho_i=rho_i^(s+1); for rho_i=0 both sides vanish because s>0. The error term is at most epsilon 2^(-i-1). Its first m weights sum to 1-2^(-m), tending to 1, so the total error is at most epsilon.

R005.fact: For finite c≥0 and Q∈[0,infinity], if c≤Q+epsilon for every real epsilon>0, then c≤Q. If c is a lower bound for every cost in a covering family, then c is at most the infimum of those costs in [0,infinity], including an empty family.

grounds.reason: c is finite and fixed by s,delta,E.
For fixed V, F004 holds for arbitrary epsilon>0.
Q=sum_i rho_i^(s+1) depends on V, not on epsilon; V is arbitrary among delta-covers.
The right-hand scale content is precisely the infimum of these covering costs.

R005.justification: For Q=infinity the assertion is immediate. For Q finite, c>Q would contradict the hypothesis with epsilon=(c-Q)/2. This removes only an auxiliary real error, without exchanging limits with covers, integrals or sums. The infimum is the greatest lower bound; if the covering family were empty its infimum is infinity and the inequality still holds.

R006.fact: For a nonempty family (a_j) in [0,infinity] with supremum A, a_j<=A for every j; if A=infinity, then for each finite real T>0 some a_j>T. Conversely an element B of [0,infinity] satisfying B>T for every finite T>0 equals infinity.

grounds.reason: H is the supremum over the nonempty family of all positive real scales, with contents in [0,infinity].
N001 establishes H^s(E)=infinity under 0<s<D; T is arbitrary positive finite.

R006.justification: These are defining least-upper-bound properties: if every a_j were <=T, then A<=T, contradicting A=infinity. Each a_j is bounded above by A. A finite B cannot exceed every positive finite T, since T=B+1 is such a bound. These facts justify the witness and the supremum steps in S001-S003.

R006.fact: If D is a finite positive real and Q in [0,infinity] satisfies Q>=s+1 for every real s with 0<s<D, then Q>=D+1. Equivalently, for every finite real b<D+1 there exists s with 0<s<D and b<s+1.

grounds.reason: D is finite and nonnegative.
L1 is D>0 and s is arbitrary under L2: 0<s<D.
F003 supplies Q=dim_H(F)>=s+1 with exactly those open assumptions.

R006.justification: For b<D+1 set a=max(0,b-1) and s=(a+D)/2. Positivity of D and b-1<D give 0<=a<D, hence 0<s<D and b-1<=a<s, so b<s+1. If Q<D+1, Q is finite and choosing b=Q contradicts Q>=s+1. If Q is infinite the claimed bound holds directly. This expands precisely the endpoint argument already given in S004.

R007.fact: For the covers in S002, diam(W_i)≤diam(V_i)≤delta, and for s>0, sum_i diam(W_i)^s≤sum_i diam(V_i)^s, including empty members and infinite total sums.

Diameters are suprema of pairwise distances with empty diameter zero.
Cover costs are countable sums of nonnegative positive powers.

R007.justification: Every pairwise distance in W_i is a distance between two points of V_i and is bounded by its diameter. Take the supremum; the empty case is zero. Positive real powers preserve order on nonnegative reals (at zero the value is zero; on positive reals this follows from the increasing logarithm and exponential). Monotonicity of each finite partial sum passes to the nonnegative series, defined as the supremum of finite subsums.

R007.fact: For each s with 0<s<1 and each delta>0, the displayed cost inequality for every delta-cover V of F implies H^s_delta(I)≤H^s_delta(F). Consequently H^s(I)≤H^s(F), as inequalities in [0,infinity].

grounds.reason: The proof constructs a cover W of I for each admissible V and bounds its cost by that of V.
Contents are infima of admissible cover costs and measures are suprema over all positive scales.

If the admissible class is empty its infimum is infinity, so the assertion still holds. Pointwise order at every positive scale implies order of the two suprema. R007.fact: If d∈[0,infinity] satisfies d≥s for every real s with 0<s<1, then d≥1.
